title: Cybersecurity Career Paths
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Cybersecurity Career Paths.
Apply cybersecurity career paths to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers cybersecurity career paths in the Introduction to Cybersecurity track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Use ordinary examples such as an email account, a laptop, or a school project to connect abstract terms to assets and consequences. The specific focus here is cybersecurity career paths; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Cybersecurity Career Paths focuses on security analyst; security engineer; penetration tester. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Security Analyst
items.text: For security analyst, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Digital Forensics Analyst
items.text: Forensic work requires a documented source, collection method, integrity verification, access log, and analysis timeline. Preserve originals, use validated tools, account for clock drift, and state limits on each conclusion.

items.title: Cloud Security Engineer
items.text: Cloud and delivery security combine least-privilege identities, hardened defaults, approved dependencies, secret management, artifact provenance, logging, and repeatable deployment checks. Verify service-specific behavior and avoid placing secrets in source or logs.

items.text: For security architect and security manager, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

content_blocks.title: Defensive example (synthetic data)
content_blocks.code:
asset = {"name": "student-laptop", "criticality": "medium", "internet_exposed": False}
print(f"asset: {asset['name']}")
print(f"criticality: {asset['criticality']}")
print(f"internet exposed: {asset['internet_exposed']}")
content_blocks.expected_output:
asset: student-laptop
criticality: medium
internet exposed: False
content_blocks.notes: This example uses synthetic values and has no network dependency. CodeLeaf displays it as instructional text; production does not execute arbitrary learner code.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Cybersecurity is a risk-management discipline: identify what matters, understand what could harm it, and choose safeguards that fit the context. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Cybersecurity Career Paths focuses on security analyst; security engineer; penetration tester. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Cybersecurity Career Paths. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Security Analyst; Security Engineer; Penetration Tester), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

asset: student-laptop
criticality: medium
internet exposed: False
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Cybersecurity Career Paths is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.

sources.title: NICE Framework Resource Center
sources.notes: Use the current NICE Framework components when mapping knowledge and skills to work roles.

sources.title: Secure by Design
sources.notes: Use as a design-practice reference, not as a certification or proof that a product is secure.
